stories.title_en: A Secret Seal-Stamp Wins a Travel Roll in Court

paragraphs.zh: 乡有尤刁民者，侮法健讼，渔猎下民。人闻其刁风，莫不畏而远之。一日，往府搭船，已先入船坐。后搭船者群至，萍水相逢，彼此各不相识，船中对坐漫谈。忽讲及按院拿刁民事。内有姓丘后生，不知尤刁民之在船也，与众曰：“闻此时本县唯尤五最刁，凡与人暂处，无不被其骗害者。若得按院除了此人，民亦安生。”尤五心中冷笑，谓“吾与尔何干，既扬我刁，又愿按院除我？此人若不白骗他一场，枉得此刁名也。”见丘生所带铺陈甚好，即取一木印，挨近其毡条白处，私打一印号于中。
paragraphs.en: In the countryside there was a man called You the Shyster, who mocked the law, loved lawsuits, and preyed on lesser people. When people heard of his litigious ways, none but feared him and kept away. One day he took a boat to the prefecture, and was already seated on board. Later passengers came in a crowd; they were chance meetings on the water, none knew one another, and they sat facing each other chatting. Suddenly the talk turned to the touring censor rounding up litigious bullies. Among them was a young man surnamed Qiu, who did not know that You the Shyster was on the boat. He said to the others: “I hear that in our county right now You Wu is the most litigious of all. Anyone who is with him even a short while is cheated and harmed. If the touring censor would get rid of this man, the people could live in peace.” You Wu laughed coldly to himself: “What have I to do with you, that you spread my shyster name and even wish the censor to get rid of me? If I do not cheat this man openly, I will have this shyster name for nothing.” He saw that Young Qiu had very fine bedding, so he took a wood seal, drew near a white place on the felt, and secretly stamped a mark in the middle.

paragraphs.zh: 船晚至岸，各收拾自己行李而去。尤刁民尾丘生之后，行至府前，在仆担头把铺陈抢下，曰：“多劳你挑，我自拖去。”丘生来抢，曰：“是我铺陈，你拖何去？”二人互争不开，打入府堂上去。尤曰：“是我物，他强争。”丘亦曰：“是他争我物。”太爷曰：“你两人互争，各有甚记号？”丘曰：“我自买来的，未作记号。”尤曰：“我毡条内打有印记。”当堂开视，尤取衣带中木印对之，果相同。太府曰：“此是尤某之物，丘何得冒争！”将丘打十板，令尤领铺陈去，各赶出府外。丘骂曰：“你这贼是何人，敢如此骗我？后必报之！”尤五曰：“适船间你说尤刁民者，即是我。我与你何干，而终日道我刁？故教训你，刁人是这等做耳！”丘心中方悔：“是我妄称人恶，故致此失也。”
paragraphs.en: In the evening the boat reached shore; each man gathered his own luggage and left. You the Shyster tagged after Young Qiu. When they came before the prefectural offices, he snatched the bedding off the servant’s carrying pole and said: “Thanks for carrying it; I will drag it myself.” Young Qiu came to snatch it back and said: “This is my bedding—where are you dragging it?” The two fought without yielding, and the fight went up into the prefectural hall. You said: “It is my thing; he is forcing a claim.” Qiu also said: “He is seizing my thing.” His Honor said: “You two each claim it; what mark does each of you have?” Qiu said: “I bought it myself; I made no mark.” You said: “I stamped a seal inside the felt.” They opened it in court; You took the wood seal from his sash and matched it, and it was the same. The prefect said: “This is You’s thing. How can Qiu falsely claim it?” He had Qiu given ten strokes, ordered You to take the bedding, and drove them both out of the offices. Qiu cursed: “You thief, who are you, that you dare cheat me like this? I will pay you back later!” You Wu said: “On the boat just now you spoke of You the Shyster—that is me. What had I to do with you, that you spent the day calling me a shyster? So I taught you a lesson: this is how a shyster works!” Only then did Qiu regret in his heart: “I spoke of a man’s evil at random, and so brought this loss on myself.”

paragraphs.zh: 按：刁恶者，人谁不憎？但未识其人，勿轻扬其过。彼或从旁听之，必致恨于心。待你有失处，乘其隙而毒之，使人不自知矣。故古人三缄其口而慎其言。庞公遗安之计，但称曰好。彼尤五虽恶，何丘后生背地谈之，而自取尤五白占铺陈？与庞公遗安之计异矣。故孔子恶称人之恶，孟氏惕言人之不善者，皆圣贤教人远怨之道，言不可不慎也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Who does not hate a litigious villain? But if you do not know the man, do not lightly spread his faults. He may be listening from the side, and will surely store hatred in his heart. When you have a weak point, he will take the opening and poison you, and you will not even know it. That is why the ancients sealed their mouths three times and were careful of their words. Pangong’s plan for leaving peace to his descendants was simply to call everyone good. You Wu was evil, to be sure; but why did young Qiu talk of him behind his back, and bring on You Wu’s open seizure of the bedding? That is a far cry from Pangong’s plan for leaving peace. So Confucius disliked those who spoke of others’ faults, and Mencius was wary of talking of others’ lack of goodness: both are the way of sages and worthies teaching people to keep far from resentment. Words must not be used carelessly.

stories.title_en: He Slaps a Plaster over the Face and Snatches an Ingot

paragraphs.zh: 县城有一银匠，家颇殷实，解户领秋粮银，常托其倾煎。一日倾煎元宝，心内尚有系未透处，夜间又煮洗之。其铺门有一大缝，外可窥见其内。一棍买一大膏药，夜间潜往窥之。见其把两元宝洗讫，放于炉边，棍在外作叫痛声，呼曰：“开门！”银匠问曰：“是谁？”棍外答曰：“被赃坯打得重，求你炉边灼一膏药贴之。”银匠开门与入。棍作瘸行状，且手战呼痛，蓬头俯视，以一大膏药在炉边灼开，把两手望银匠当面一贴，即抢一元宝以逃。银匠不胜热痛，急扯下膏药，元宝已被其窃一去矣。急叫：“有贼！”且出门追赶，不知从哪路去。彷徨追过数十步，只得怅恨而归。
paragraphs.en: In the county town there was a silversmith, fairly well off. The tax-silver handlers who took in the autumn-grain silver often trusted him to melt and cast it. One day he was melting sycee ingots; some spots inside were still not fully worked through, so at night he boiled and washed them again. The shop door had a large crack; from outside one could see in. A crook bought a large plaster and at night crept up to peek. He saw the man finish washing two ingots and set them by the furnace. The crook outside made sounds of pain and called: “Open the door!” The silversmith asked: “Who is it?” The crook answered from outside: “I was beaten badly by a dirty brute. I beg you to let me heat a plaster by your furnace and stick it on.” The silversmith opened the door and let him in. The crook pretended to limp, and with shaking hands cried pain, hair in a mess, looking down. He heated a large plaster by the furnace until it opened, slapped it with both hands straight onto the silversmith’s face, then grabbed one ingot and fled. The silversmith could not bear the burning pain; he hurriedly tore the plaster off, but one ingot had already been stolen. He shouted, “Thief!” and went out to chase, but did not know which way the man had gone. He ran in confusion for several dozen steps, then could only go home sick with hate.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍装痛呼门及炉边灼膏药，情果难察。但元宝重物，须先收藏，然后开门则可无失矣。后人观此，凡有银在身者，皆不可轻容异色人得近旁也。
paragraphs.en: Note: This crook pretended to be in pain, called for the door, and heated a plaster by the furnace—the manner was indeed hard to see through. But an ingot is a heavy thing; he ought first to have put it away, and then opened the door, and there would have been no loss. Later readers, looking at this: anyone who has silver on him must not lightly let a strange-looking person come near.

stories.title_en: A Thief Blinds Them with Lime and Takes the Packets

paragraphs.zh: 孙滔，河南人也。常买绵布，在福建建宁府卖。一夜，在银匠王六店煎银，倾煎已讫，时对二包在桌。二人复在对银，有一盗径入其铺，将石灰撒其目。二人救目不暇，盗即将桌上所包之银拿走。滔拼命赶去，将及，盗乃丢一包于地。滔拾包归，到银铺开视之，则皆铁矣。后竟无迹可捕也。
paragraphs.en: Sun Tao was a man of Henan. He often bought cotton cloth and sold it in Jianning Prefecture in Fujian. One night he was at silversmith Wang Liu’s shop melting silver. The melting was done, and two packets sat facing each other on the table. The two men were still checking the silver when a thief walked straight into the shop and threw lime into their eyes. The two had no time but to save their eyes; the thief took the packaged silver off the table and left. Tao chased with all his life. He was about to catch him when the thief dropped one packet on the ground. Tao picked up the packet and went back; when he opened it at the silversmith’s, it was all iron. After that there was no trace by which to catch him.

paragraphs.zh: 按：语云：“贼是小人，智过君子。”诚哉是言也！其始入铺，撒灰腌人之目，致人无暇顾其财；追将近身、丢包于地，乃杜赶以脱其身也。此岂贼窥伺之机熟，而慢藏诲盗？然滔之不谨于其素，有以致之矣。鉴此惩噎，是为得之。
paragraphs.en: Note: The saying goes, “A thief is a small man, but his wit outruns a gentleman.” How true that is! When he first entered the shop, he threw lime to sting their eyes, so they had no time to look to their money; when the chase had nearly reached him, he dropped a packet on the ground, to stop the pursuit and slip away. Was this only because the thief’s watching and waiting were ripe, and careless storage invites thieves? Yet Tao’s usual want of care had brought it on. Take this as a warning from choking, and you will have it right.

stories.title_en: Crooks Strip Him at the Latrine in Open Day

paragraphs.zh: 王亨，南京扬州府人，是本府典吏。二考已满，该上京办事。家贫无措，措借亲朋银十馀两，独往北京，为办事使用。始到京中，在教军场边草坪中大解。方脱下裤，陡被二棍拿住，且骂且剥曰：“你这贼偷我衣物来。”即把其衣服并银一时抢去逃走。待他起来，缚裤赶之，二棍逃已远矣。亨行路日久，力已疲倦，拼死赶他不上，懊恨冲天，只得在会同馆乞借盘缠回家，另作区处。
paragraphs.en: Wang Heng was a man of Yangzhou Prefecture under Nanjing, a clerk in that prefecture. His two terms of clerical service were up, and he was due to go to the capital for assignment. The family was poor and had no means; he borrowed a little more than ten taels from kin and friends and went alone to Beijing, for use in the assignment. Just after he reached the capital, he was relieving himself on the grass by the drill ground. He had just dropped his trousers when two crooks seized him, cursing and stripping him: “You thief, you stole our clothes.” They snatched his clothes and silver at once and ran. By the time he got up, tied his trousers, and chased them, the two crooks were already far off. Heng had been on the road many days and was worn out; he chased with all his life and could not catch them. Sick with hate that filled the sky, he could only go to the Huitongguan guesthouse and beg travel money to go home, and make other plans later.

paragraphs.zh: 按：孤客出外，非唯僻处可防劫夺，即大路解手之际，必当以裤脱之，挟在腋下。倘遇光棍若行歹意，则起而逃之亦可，或与之交战亦可。若王亨者，不知提防，而被棍将衣银尽剥一空。斯时也，盘缠无觅，顾何前程？苟非会同馆中同道辈乞借盘缠而归，几为乞丐矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: A lone traveler abroad should guard against robbery not only in lonely places. Even on a main road, when relieving himself, he must take the trousers off and hold them under his arm. If crooks then mean harm, he can get up and run, or he can fight them. As for Wang Heng, he did not know to guard, and the crooks stripped him of clothes and silver down to nothing. At that moment he had no travel money to find—what of his future post? If fellow clerks at the Huitongguan had not lent him travel money to go home, he would nearly have become a beggar.
